headings.title: Introduction to Primary Nursing
headings.content: Primary nursing is a professional care delivery model designed to facilitate continuous, comprehensive, and coordinated nursing care for hospitalized patients. Developed in the 1970s by Marie Manthey, this model establishes a direct relationship between a single designated nurse, known as the primary nurse, and an assigned patient throughout their entire hospital stay. Unlike task-oriented methods where different nurses perform fragmented duties like medication administration, vital signs, or hygiene care, primary nursing empowers one registered nurse to take 24-hour accountability for planning, executing, and evaluating the patient's individualized care plan from admission to discharge. When the primary nurse is off duty, associate nurses follow the established plan of care to ensure seamless continuity. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice, understanding primary nursing is crucial because it promotes high-quality, patient-centered care and fosters deep therapeutic nurse-patient relationships. It elevates professional accountability, enhances job satisfaction, and reduces errors by minimizing communication breakdowns among healthcare team members. By holding total responsibility for patient outcomes during the hospital episode, the primary nurse acts as the central coordinator communicating with physicians, pharmacists, and families. This model highlights the autonomous role of the registered nurse and serves as a gold standard in many advanced clinical environments globally.

headings.title: Core Principles and Philosophy of Primary Nursing
headings.content: The core principles and philosophy of primary nursing revolve around decentralization of decision-making, direct nurse-to-patient accountability, and collaborative teamwork. At its heart, the model believes that the registered nurse best equipped to care for a patient is the one who establishes a continuous, trust-based relationship with them from the moment of entry into the healthcare facility. Decision-making authority is placed directly at the bedside with the nurse caring for the patient, rather than resting with distant nursing administrators or head nurses. This decentralization fosters rapid clinical responses and highly personalized interventions tailored to the patient's unique physical, psychological, and cultural needs. Continuity of care is another foundational pillar; patients do not have to repeatedly explain their histories to a revolving door of different caregivers, which significantly reduces patient anxiety and builds trust. Collaboration is also vital, as the primary nurse acts as the primary advocate and spokesperson for the patient during multidisciplinary rounds. For nursing students, internalizing these principles means recognizing that professional nursing transcends routine tasks; it requires total ownership of clinical outcomes, moral agency, and an unwavering commitment to advocacy. By upholding these core tenets, nurses elevate the profession's standing and ensure that patient safety and dignity remain at the forefront of clinical delivery.

headings.title: Roles and Responsibilities of the Primary Nurse
headings.content: The roles and responsibilities of the primary nurse are extensive, demanding a high level of clinical competence, leadership, and organization. Upon a patient's admission, the primary nurse conducts a comprehensive nursing assessment, identifies priority nursing diagnoses, and formulates an individualized plan of care. This plan must remain dynamic, reflecting the patient's changing health status day by day. When the primary nurse is off duty, they communicate the care plan details to associate nurses through thorough shift reports and documented care guidelines, ensuring that care remains consistent 24 hours a day. Another crucial responsibility is acting as the central coordinator and advocate. The primary nurse collaborates closely with physicians, physiotherapists, dietitians, and social workers to streamline treatments and discharge planning. Patient and family education is also a core duty; because the primary nurse knows the patient best, they are uniquely positioned to assess learning readiness, deliver tailored health teachings, and evaluate comprehension before discharge. For nursing students, stepping into the primary nurse mindset means embracing total patient advocacy, honing communication skills, and accepting accountability for every facet of the patient's in-hospital journey, from basic comfort measures to complex clinical management.

headings.title: Comparison with Other Nursing Care Delivery Models
headings.content: To fully appreciate primary nursing, student nurses must compare it with other traditional care delivery models such as functional nursing and team nursing. Functional nursing is a task-oriented approach where specific duties—such as administering medications, taking temperatures, or dressing wounds—are assigned to specific nurses or nursing assistants for all patients on the ward. While efficient in terms of speed during staff shortages, functional nursing leads to fragmented care, poor communication, and a lack of holistic understanding of the patient, as no single nurse knows the whole clinical picture. Team nursing, on the other hand, involves a team leader (usually a registered nurse) directing a group of staff members (RNs, ENs, and auxiliary nurses) who provide care to a group of patients together. Although team nursing promotes collaboration, it can still suffer from diffusion of responsibility and delegation confusion. Primary nursing stands apart from both by eliminating fragmented task distribution and team dilution; one registered nurse is personally accountable for the entire care episode. Studies consistently show that primary nursing increases professional satisfaction, enhances accountability, and improves patient satisfaction scores compared to functional or team models. However, it requires a fully registered nurse workforce and higher staffing ratios, which can make it resource-intensive to implement in understaffed environments.

headings.title: Implementation of Primary Nursing in Medical-Surgical Settings
headings.content: Implementing primary nursing in medical-surgical settings requires careful planning, administrative support, and a cultural shift within the healthcare institution. Med-surg units are typically fast-paced, high-turnover environments where patients present with diverse, complex multi-system conditions. To successfully transition a med-surg ward to primary nursing, hospital management must ensure an adequate mix of registered nurses, as associate nurses are needed to cover off-shift hours while maintaining the primary nurse's care plan. The implementation process begins with thorough staff orientation, education on autonomy, and reallocating nursing duties away from non-nursing chores like housekeeping or clerical work, allowing RNs to focus strictly on direct patient care. Nurse managers play a pivotal role by empowering staff, encouraging decentralized decision-making, and providing mentorship in care planning and multidisciplinary collaboration. Scheduling must also be optimized so that primary nurses are assigned patients upon admission and maintain that assignment as long as the patient remains in the unit. For nursing students undertaking clinical rotations in med-surg wards, observing this implementation reveals how structural organization directly influences patient safety, timely interventions, and the overall therapeutic climate of the hospital environment.

headings.title: Advantages and Challenges in Patient Outcomes
headings.content: The adoption of primary nursing yields profound advantages for patient outcomes, though it also introduces distinct operational challenges. On the positive side, patient outcomes include significantly reduced lengths of stay, lower rates of hospital-acquired complications like pressure ulcers and falls, higher patient satisfaction scores, and smoother transitions from hospital to home. Because the primary nurse closely monitors subtle clinical changes, deterioration is caught and managed much earlier. Nurses themselves experience higher job satisfaction, greater professional autonomy, and enhanced skill mastery. However, the challenges are notable. Primary nursing demands a 100% registered nurse staffing model or a very high RN-to-patient ratio, which can be costly and difficult to maintain during nursing shortages. Burnout and emotional exhaustion can also occur if primary nurses carry heavy caseloads of critically ill patients without adequate rest breaks or institutional support. Furthermore, scheduling conflicts can arise when trying to match patient admissions with the primary nurse's working days off. For nursing students, weighing these advantages against challenges teaches critical administrative thinking, preparing them to advocate for sustainable staffing models that protect both patient safety and nurse well-being in their future careers.

headings.title: Relevance and Application within the Nigerian Healthcare System
headings.content: Examining the relevance and application of primary nursing within the Nigerian healthcare system highlights both immense potential and unique structural hurdles. Nigeria's healthcare sector often contends with severe nursing shortages, brain drain ('japa' syndrome), high patient-to-nurse ratios, and resource-constrained clinical environments. In many Nigerian tertiary and secondary hospitals, traditional functional or team nursing models predominate due to these staffing realities. Yet, applying primary nursing principles—even in modified forms—offers transformative benefits for Nigerian patient care. Encouraging individual nurses to take personal ownership of assigned patients can drastically improve clinical vigilance, reduce medication errors, and foster better rapport with patients who often experience anxiety navigating complex public hospital systems. To adapt primary nursing locally, hospital managements must advocate for task-shifting (delegating non-nursing duties to ward orderlies and clerks), improve working conditions to retain registered nurses, and foster interprofessional collaboration. For nursing students trained in Nigeria, understanding how to apply primary nursing concepts within local constraints is invaluable. It equips future nursing leaders with the innovative mindset needed to advocate for policy changes, optimize available human resources, and elevate the quality of professional nursing care across Nigerian hospitals.
